Wusool Engine go-live plan

2026-11-10 · Sinan Shamsudheen

MCP v1 shipped first and reached prod on 15 Nov, ahead of the planned 20 Nov. Then eight phases from 23 Nov to 12 Mar take the Engine prototype live on our Core API in the order of the Before and After rollout. Each phase ends with one flow advisors can use and give feedback on. Sinan connects what already exists into each flow; Abhay builds the missing modules one phase ahead. Richu, our database engineer, sets up the tables for every phase at once, so both developers build on a ready database. Every screen and action in the prototype now maps to a phase (see Feature coverage).

Roadmap

Read each column top down: what Abhay builds supports what Sinan wires up, and that delivers the flow advisors get at the end of the phase.

The PDF's monthly rollout dates the Wusool MCP's tools, not the Engine's screens. The MCP foundation with the buyer and seller tools ships first, before phase 0 (see MCP v1). Covering every page of the prototype, including Home, documents, scorecards and partners, takes the plan to 12 Mar.

MCP v1: the first release (in prod 15 Nov)

Before the rest of the plan, advisors get the Wusool MCP: add, edit and bulk-upload buyers and sellers from Claude. A bulk list is previewed and confirmed in Claude before anything is created. v1 runs on today's backend, with no /api/v1 endpoints, no crm move, and one migration for its CRM tools, to let command_runs record mcp. The benchmark tools added two tables of their own (see below). The tools, sign-in and foundation are specified in AZM-168, which is done. Phase 0 can start.

  • Look-ups: get_buyer, get_seller, list_buyers, list_sellers (up to 50, with filters), check_buyer and list_field_options.

  • Benchmark: the GCC SME Benchmark's peer anchors, revenue bands and metric weights moved from code into two Postgres tables, owned by a new benchmark_data module. Advisors read and edit them from Claude; each edit is checked and live at once. Rows keep the editor's Slack user id and name, and old values are not kept yet.

  • Audit and sign-in: every call leaves an mcp.tool_called activity. Slack sign-in moved into a new auth module shared with the web app; the MCP still signs in with Slack.

Done, in prod since 15 Nov: a buyer and a seller added and edited from Claude, and a 140-row list confirmed in Claude lands in Attio.

Phase 0: Database (Richu, 23 Nov–11 Dec)

The only errors left are what Richu sets up himself: the pg_cron extension, the PGMQ install and the wusool_owner role. Nine indexes that used created_at on tables without it are fixed: eight tables now declare the column. The valuation file loads into the new market tables as it is (see Valuation data move in the Database guide). Migrations only for now; the backfill runs in report mode in the week of 1 Dec and writes on 15 Dec, with the Attio data migration. RDS offers Postgres 18 and prod and dev can upgrade to it directly from 16.13.

Richu upgrades the database to Postgres 18 and builds every table the prototype needs in one pass, following the Database guide and DDL tabs, which hold the conventions, the full DDL (16 Alembic revisions, 13 schemas), the Attio mapping, the indexes and the migration steps. Phase 0 starts once MCP v1 is in prod (see MCP v1), with the tables for phases 1 to 3 first, so no phase waits on the database. Migrations reach dev and prod only through the deploy workflow, never from a laptop; when a later phase finds a gap, Richu adds the follow-up migration. Database rules every phase relies on

  • Buyers and sellers are always roles. A mandate's client, every counterparty and every search-list entry points at a buyer role or seller role, never at a copy of its details. The database refuses a row without the right role for the mandate's side or the list's purpose.

  • Nothing is hard-deleted. Records a person can remove get removed_at; every read filters on it, and uniqueness ignores removed rows.

  • Metadata everywhere. created_at and updated_at on every table (the trigger keeps updated_at honest), created_by and updated_by where a person edits.

  • Immutable history. Every input is stored byte-for-byte, with its SHA-256, in audit.raw_inputs, forever. Every write records an event in audit.events, and a trigger stores the old and new value of each changed field in audit.record_changes; an update without an event is refused.

  • Reporting reads analytics. Dashboards and the weekly meeting read precomputed views refreshed every 10 minutes; live screens read the working tables through their indexes.

  • Nothing from today is lost. activities is copied into audit.events; tool_runs, command_runs, matching, discovery and enrichment tables are kept and re-keyed; the Attio mirror is backfilled into core.

Access control. Roles (admin, advisor, analyst, ops) grant permissions; users hold roles in core.user_roles; deal access comes from core.mandate_team, so an analyst sees only deals they are staffed on and ops sees no deal pages. The API checks core.v_user_permissions on every request.

One usage ledger for every provider. Apollo, Diffbot, PDL, Firecrawl, Google Places, Apify, Bedrock and web search all write to usage.ledger (amount in the provider's unit, USD cost, tokens, latency, the Engine job, who approved it). usage.budgets sets a monthly limit per provider per user, and Apollo cannot be charged without a named approver. The same ledger answers "what does each AI job cost per month".

Every claim has a source. Any value from an outside source (Diffbot, PDL, Firecrawl, Google Places, Apollo, LinkedIn, Gmail, Scribe) and any AI-written sentence (blurbs, brief lines, Scribe summary points, match reasons, proposed changes) is saved with a citation: an audit.evidence row pointing at the exact passage of its raw input. The database refuses a claim without one. On the web, any value or sentence can open a source chip showing the quote, the link, when it was captured and the original input, even if the website has since changed.

Each takes the kind (transaction, VC round or listed). A comp added or edited by an advisor is verified by that advisor and counts in the median at once; a bulk import stays unverified until someone verifies it. Then rewire the backend in one step: writers go to the new tables first with the Attio outbox updating Attio, readers move to the new tables, the dual-write helper is deleted, and the old public tables are frozen. Reports in the Engine: Sanity Studio inside the app

Today the Reports link under Firm opens www.sanity.io/manage in a new tab, and the real Studio is hosted separately at wusool-reports.sanity.studio. The goal is to keep people inside the Engine: Reports opens the Sanity Studio at /studio on the Engine's own address, with the Engine's left nav still on screen.

Why embed, not frame or rebuild. The hosted Studio cannot be shown in an iframe: it redirects to www.sanity.io, which sends x-frame-options: sameorigin and a frame-ancestors list of Sanity domains only (checked 13 Nov). Rebuilding the editor on the Sanity API would mean redoing rich text, images, drafts and publishing. The Studio is a React component, so the Engine renders it as a page, the same way a Next.js site mounts it at /studio.

Sign-in. The first time someone opens /studio in a browser, Sanity asks them to log in with their Sanity account and returns them to /studio; the session is remembered after that. Editors can pick Google as their Sanity login, using the address invited to the project. Passing the Engine's own sign-in through to Sanity would need Sanity SSO, an Enterprise feature we do not have. Editors stay members of the Sanity project.

Partners. If the website's partner documents live in a different Sanity project from itidwo8t, the same Studio shows both as two workspaces, /studio/reports and /studio/website.

Event engine and queue

We adopt PGMQ in phase 1, with a typed queue module and a small event engine on top of it. Every job and every change sent to Attio then survives a restart and runs in order per record.

  • Queue module. Each queue is declared as Queue[T] with a Pydantic payload. Each message is an Event[T] with a UUIDv7 id and an ordering key. The module wraps pgmq-py's SQLAlchemy async client (SQLAlchemyAsyncPGMQueue, checked in pgmq-py 1.1.4) on our own engine, so a send joins the record change's transaction through its conn argument. It sends the ordering key as PGMQ's FIFO group (x-pgmq-group), read with read_grouped, so messages with the same key never run together or out of order: PGMQ skips a group while an earlier message in it is in flight. Only attio_outbox (grouped by Attio record) and scheduled_jobs (grouped by job name, so a slow run never overlaps the next) read grouped. Every other queue uses a plain read, because messages without a group header all share one default group and would run one at a time. Workers long-poll with pgmq-py's with_poll reads, so we write no LISTEN/NOTIFY code. A message can be delayed with available_at. A permanent failure is archived for inspection.

  • Event engine. Every input is first stored byte-for-byte, with its SHA-256, in audit.raw_inputs. Every write then records one row in audit.events (who, when, which records, the source link) and, through a trigger, the old and new value of each changed field in audit.record_changes. The event, the field changes and the outbox message (only the record to sync, not the change) commit in the same transaction as the record change, and projectors update other tables from new events. There is no workflow engine such as Temporal, because every job in this plan is a single step.

  • Queues we need:

QueuePhaseDoes
import_jobs2Processes bulk imports and discovery finds into staging
attio_outbox3Writes a changed record's current state from Postgres to Attio: one write per record, with queued repeats for the same record folded into it, retried on failure
gmail_sync, calendar_sync4, 5The interactions poll pass (every 15 minutes, through domain-wide delegation) puts each mailbox's new mail and calendar changes here, so every item is retried, counted and alerted on its own
enrichment_jobs4Runs approved enrichment and Apollo calls
outreach_followups4Delayed messages at 4 and 9 working days; the worker first checks that no reply has arrived
briefs5Builds and sends the 07:30 brief per user
document_jobs6Generates engagement documents and watches Drive folders
dataroom_events7Ingests VantageKit activity
nudges7Slack alerts for overdue next steps, replies and NDAs signed
scheduled_jobs1pg_cron puts one message here per schedule for jobs with no queue of their own: the 15-minute mail and calendar poll pass, the nightly Attio resync, the weekly scorecard snapshot and Drive watch renewal; grouped by job name, so a run never overlaps the previous one

Scheduled jobs. pg_cron runs inside Postgres and only sends a message to a PGMQ queue; the worker does the job. A job that already has a queue gets its message there: the 07:30 Dubai brief is a pg_cron entry at 03:30 UTC (Dubai has no daylight saving) sending to briefs, and the daily overdue check sends to nudges. The rest go to the one scheduled_jobs queue, whose payload names the job. Because the schedule runs once in the database, two app instances never run a job twice, and the poll loop with an advisory lock in interactions/bootstrap.py retires. Schedules are created in Alembic migrations, like the PGMQ install.

PGMQ replaces only the job runner, which today is an in-process asyncio.create_task. Duplicate-request checks and rate limits still move into ordinary Postgres tables. PGMQ installs as plain SQL through Alembic, so it should run on RDS without an extension; Richu confirms this with the install migration in week 1, using the SQL bundled with pgmq-py (PGMQ 1.13.0, which has the FIFO read functions). A SQL-only install cannot be upgraded in place, so a newer PGMQ is a new migration.

Retries. PGMQ retries on its own only through the visibility timeout: a message that is not deleted in time becomes readable again, and read_ct counts the attempts. The queue module adds the rest, and each queue declares its own limits:

  • Attempt limit: once read_ct passes the limit, the message moves to a failed queue instead of running again.

  • Blocked groups: in a grouped queue, a failing message holds back the later messages for the same key until it succeeds or reaches the attempt limit. It then moves to the failed queue, the rest continue, and the alert names the record. For attio_outbox nothing is lost: a message only names the record to sync, so the next successful write carries the latest state. A worker handles a batch's messages for one key in order and stops that key at the first failure.

  • Backoff: after a failure the handler sets a growing delay with set_vt, rather than waiting out the fixed timeout each time.

  • Permanent errors: a validation failure is archived at once and never retried.

  • Alerts: failed-queue counts are reported, so a stuck attio_outbox is noticed.

  • Safe repeats: a retry can repeat a Gmail send or an Apollo call, so the handler first checks that the action has not already happened, for example that the touchpoint is not already recorded.

Inbound handlers. Two rules for every handler that reads from Attio, Gmail, Calendar, VantageKit, Scribe or a provider:

  • Idempotent on the source's key. It upserts by the source's own record id (attio_record_id, gmail_message_id, google_event_id, vantagekit_event_id and so on), so the same item arriving twice changes nothing, and it carries the raw_input_id into the event it writes.

  • Replay is re-running the handler. Each handler has a handler_version; after a fix we bump it and re-run the handler over the raw inputs it processed with an older version. Raw inputs are kept forever, so nothing is lost, and the event log shows what the replay changed.

We do not add a separate facts and projectors layer: with a few clean sources and stable record ids, these two rules give the same guarantees.

Module ownership

Every table has exactly one owning module in server/app/modules/; only that module writes it. Other modules read or change it through the owner's application service, never by importing its persistence code, and the architecture tests enforce that. Foreign keys may cross modules, because integrity belongs in the database. A schema can hold tables from more than one module.

Each new module ships with its README, __all__, and a line in the repo-wide architecture test, in the phase that first uses it.

API design

Each module owns its own HTTP API next to the tables it owns, built the same way in every module; engine only composes the multi-module page reads. Every endpoint below replaces one or more prototype functions, and its operation_id is named after that function so the generated client lines up with the swap.

application/Use cases: one function per action, typed in and out
persistence/Repositories and ORM models; never imported by a router

Ground rules

  • Postgres becomes the record, behind an API that does not change. Endpoints are shaped as mandates and counterparties from the first day. They read from the old tables until the 15 Dec migration, then from our own tables, so the Engine screens never change.

  • One entry point per action. Slack commands and the web call the same Core command, so dedupe and event logging happen in one place.

  • Who owns each record after the switch. Once Postgres owns an object, an edit made in Attio goes to staging for review instead of overwriting Postgres; otherwise the nightly resync would quietly undo our changes.

  • Going live means swapping function bodies. Each live function keeps the demo function's name, inputs and return shape (PRD rule). A broken connection empties one block, not the whole page.

  • The Engine's rules apply everywhere: AI never sends, no enrichment without a click, no fees on a screen that can be shared, actions in 3 clicks or fewer.

  • Repo gates: checks.sh and the architecture tests stay green, Richu writes and runs every Alembic migration, and GitBook is updated in the same PR.

  • Out of scope here: MCP tools beyond buyers and sellers (see MCP v1), and new screens, which Jules and Ramzy build unless we agree otherwise.

Build rules: libraries before hand-written code

These apply to every phase. Before writing a helper for a problem a library already solves, check this table. A new library gets a row here in the same PR. Existing helpers (utilities/domain/retry.py, the Attio and Google retry wrappers, enrichment/providers/http_json.py, utilities/tests/bedrock_fakes.py) move to these when their files are next touched, not in a rewrite PR.

Kept hand-written, on purpose: rate limits and duplicate-request checks as Postgres tables (rate-limit libraries need Redis); the audit trigger and outbox in one transaction; the comps median (statistics); Cmd+K on pg_trgm and full-text search; the Attio, Apollo, VantageKit and Sanity clients on httpx and Pydantic, since none has a good Python SDK. Not adopted: Celery, Dramatiq, Redis, APScheduler and Temporal; PGMQ and pg_cron cover every job in this plan.

Database guide

Richu builds one normalised Postgres 18 database that holds every record the Engine shows, stays field-for-field in step with Attio prod, and is ready before each phase needs it. This tab is the guide; the DDL tab holds the tables to implement.

Decisions and conventions

Every table follows these rules; a migration that breaks one is sent back in review.

TopicRuleWhy
EnginePostgreSQL 18 on RDS, upgraded from 16 with a blue/green deploymentNative uuidv7(), virtual generated columns, faster upgrades and skip-scan on composite indexes
Primary keysid uuid PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT uuidv7() on every tableTime-ordered ids keep inserts local in the index, and our ids never depend on Attio
Outside idsTheir own column with a unique constraint: attio_record_id, attio_entry_id, gmail_message_id, sanity_document_idOutside systems change or retire; our keys stay
Fixed choicesA lookup table in ref with a code text key, never a Postgres ENUMAttio select options change; a row is easy to add, rename or retire
Several valuesA junction table with foreign keys, never an arrayArrays cannot hold a foreign key, so sectors and geographies drift
MoneyOne *_usd numeric(18,2) columnNo floating point. All money is stored in USD; a non-USD figure is converted when it is entered, using ref.fx_rates (Gulf pegs such as AED 3.6725 and SAR 3.75; a dated rate for EUR, GBP or EGP, kept in fx_rate_on). The one exception is offers: an LOI keeps its figure and currency exactly as written, plus enterprise_value_usd for comparing offers
Percentagesnumeric(5,2) with CHECK (x BETWEEN 0 AND 100)One scale everywhere
Timetimestamptz for instants, date for calendar days (deadlines, FY)Every instant is written in UTC: the database and both login roles run with timezone = 'UTC', and the app only accepts timezone-aware datetimes, converted to UTC before writing. Dubai time (UTC+4) is applied on display only. A date is a calendar day in Dubai business terms (a due date, an NDA date, a fiscal year) and is never shifted: converting a Dubai morning to UTC would move it to the previous day. When a date comes from an instant, it is taken in Asia/Dubai
Texttext, with a CHECK (length(...) <= n) only where a limit is realNo varchar(255) by habit
Emails and domainscitext, stored lower-case, unique case-insensitivelyOne person, one email; one company, one domain
Required valuesNOT NULL unless the business allows a gap; empty strings blocked with CHECK (x <> '')Rules in the database survive scripts and admin fixes
Soft deleteRecords people can remove get removed_at timestamptz (null = live): organisations, people, roles, mandates, counterparties, lists and entries, notes, offers, comps, metrics, skills, workstreams. Every read filters removed_at IS NULL, and unique rules are partial indexes WHERE removed_at IS NULL, so a removed row never blocks a new one. Logs, queues and join rows have no removed_at: logs are never deleted, and join rows are deleted with an event writtenThe PDF's rule: nothing is hard-deleted
Foreign keysEvery one has an explicit ON DELETE (RESTRICT for records, CASCADE for owned children, SET NULL for optional links) and an index on the referencing columnPostgres does not index foreign keys for you
Audit columnscreated_at, updated_at (kept current by the util.set_updated_at() trigger), and created_by / updated_by where a person editsDEFAULT now() alone never updates
JSONRaw inputs are exact bytes (bytea plus SHA-256) in audit.raw_inputs, never jsonb. jsonb only for our own typed detail that varies by kind (audit.events.detail, intake.search_runs.filters), validated by Pydantic; anything filtered, joined or constrained is a columnjsonb reorders keys and drops whitespace, so it cannot prove what a sender sent or re-check a webhook signature; matches the repo's type-safety rule
Namingsnake_case, plural tables, constraints named pk_, fk_, uq_, ck_, indexes ix_Readable errors and Alembic diffs
TenancyOne firm, so no tenant column; the database is never reachable from a browser, so no row-level securityAccess is checked in the API
MigrationsAlembic only, one revision per DDL block, each with a real downgrade(); indexes on live tables built CONCURRENTLYThe repo's rule: schema changes only through Alembic

Metadata on every table. created_at and updated_at (timestamptz, set by default and by the util.set_updated_at() trigger) on every table; created_by and updated_by on every record a person edits; removed_at for soft delete where a person can remove a record (see the Soft delete row). Append-only logs carry created_at only.

Analytics close together. Dashboard and report numbers (pipeline summary, time in stage, the deal funnel, reply rates) are materialised views in one analytics schema, refreshed every 10 minutes. Hot screens read through covering indexes (INCLUDE) so the answer comes from the index without touching the table.

Access control. Roles grant permissions, users hold roles, and deal access comes from the deal team; no role or is_admin column on users.

TableHolds
ref.rolesadmin, advisor, analyst, ops
ref.permissionsdeals.view_all, deals.view_staffed, deals.edit, outreach.send, approvals.decide, providers.spend, fees.view, skills.edit, partners.publish, users.manage, imports.approve
ref.role_permissionsWhich role grants which permission (PRD: advisors see every deal; analysts only deals they are staffed on; ops no deal pages; fees only to advisors in the engagement-letter dialog)
core.user_rolesWhich roles each person holds, who granted them and when
core.mandate_teamWho works on each deal (advisor or analyst); advisors sync to Attio's assigned advisor
core.v_user_permissionsThe permission set the API checks on every request

The database is never reachable from a browser, so the API enforces these on every call; every grant and change is an event like any other write.

One usage ledger for every provider. Apollo, Diffbot, PDL, Firecrawl, Google Places, Apify, Bedrock and web search all write to usage.ledger: provider, user, the person who approved it, operation, the Engine job, model, quoted and actual amount in the provider's unit, USD cost, tokens, latency, and the raw response. usage.budgets sets a monthly limit per provider per user (or firm-wide), and usage.v_budget_remaining drives the credit preview and the refusal above budget. A provider marked requires_approval (Apollo) cannot be charged without a named approver. The same ledger gives the PRD's monthly AI cost per job.

Schemas and relationships

Thirteen Postgres schemas follow the backend modules. core holds the records Attio also holds, and every other schema references core. core points outward only through three optional, nullable links (a mandate's source partner, a counterparty's search candidate, a note's meeting), each added after the target table exists.

A counterparty belongs to exactly one mandate or one prospect list (enforced by a check), and offers, data room links and drafts reach a mandate only through it. ref (lookups) and pgmq (queues) sit outside the picture.

Buyers and sellers are always roles. A company's buyer or seller details live once, in core.buyer_roles or core.seller_roles. Everywhere a company takes part as a buyer or seller, the row points at that role, never at a copy of its details, and the database refuses a row without one.

Where a buyer or seller appearsMust point atEnforced by
Mandate clientSell-side: the client's seller role. Buy-side: the client's buyer role (or, for an individual, the person)CHECK on side
Counterparty on a mandateSell-side mandate: a buyer role. Buy-side mandate: a seller role (the target)Composite key (mandate_id, mandate_side) plus a CHECK
Counterparty or entry on a search listSellers list: a seller role. Buyers list: a buyer roleComposite key (list_id, looking_for) plus a CHECK
Search list serving a clientBuy-side mandate: looking for sellers. Sell-side mandate: looking for buyersComposite key (mandate_id, mandate_side) plus a CHECK
Search result marked "added"The role it becameCHECK on status
Approved import rowThe organisation, and its role for a buyer or seller importCHECK on status
Role and company togetherThe role belongs to that same companyComposite key (role_id, organization_id) to the role's UNIQUE (id, organization_id)

So "add to a deal" from Search or a universe always creates or reuses the role first, then the counterparty, in one transaction. Offers, data room links, drafts and touchpoints reach a buyer or seller only through the counterparty, so they inherit the rule. Comps are the one exception: their target and acquirer are market data, not our buyers or sellers, so they point at organisations.

Immutable history. Four kinds of table record what happened, and none of them can be edited or deleted (util.forbid_change() refuses it):

LayerTableHolds
What arrivedaudit.raw_inputsEvery input exactly as received, forever: Attio, VantageKit and Sanity webhooks, Gmail and Calendar pushes, lead-tool submissions, uploads, Claude imports, Apollo, Google Places, Firecrawl and Bedrock responses, Scribe uploads. Stored as exact bytes with a SHA-256, never as re-encoded JSON. Processing state lives apart in audit.raw_input_processing
What happenedaudit.eventsOne row per action: who (person, system, AI or Attio), when, which mandate, counterparty, company or person, the source link and any decision reason
What changedaudit.record_changesOld and new value of every field changed by each event, captured by a trigger on every record table; an update without an event is refused
Activity logscomms.email_messages, comms.touchpoints, comms.classifier_feedback, usage.ledger, work.notifications, work.notification_actions, docs.skill_versions, dataroom.activityEach send, reply, contact, credit spend, alert and response, skill version and data room view

Tables that hold current state (mandates, counterparties, approvals, drafts, stage and status history) change as work moves, and their history is the events and field changes above.

Inbound handlers are idempotent and replayable.

  • Every handler that turns a raw input into records upserts on the source's own record key (attio_record_id, attio_entry_id, gmail_message_id, google_event_id, vantagekit_event_id, apollo_person_id), so a repeated delivery changes nothing. The event it writes carries the raw_input_id.

  • audit.raw_input_processing records which handler and which handler_version processed each input. Replay after a fix is re-running that handler over a range of raw inputs whose handler_version is older; the event log and field changes show exactly what the replay changed. There is no separate facts layer: raw inputs plus these keys give the same guarantees at our volume.

Every email and meeting is linked to one counterparty. Last contact, the deal funnel and reply rates read comms.touchpoints by counterparty_id, so a message that misses the link is invisible to them. Gmail sync links each message in this order, on every mailbox the interactions engine reads, so a buyer replying to a teammate still updates the Buyers tab:

  1. The thread's earlier messages are linked: use the same deal or deals (their touchpoints). email_threads.counterparty_id is set only while a thread is on exactly one deal.

  2. Match the people: a sender or recipient in core.person_emails who is in core.counterparty_contacts of an open counterparty (status not terminal, not removed), or in core.mandate_contacts of an open mandate. A client match links to the mandate with no counterparty.

  3. Match the company: the sender's domain in core.organization_domains, against that organisation's open counterparties. Free-mail domains such as gmail.com never match.

  4. Several matches: a deal's code name (core.code_names) in the subject or body picks that deal (link_source = 'code_name').

  5. One match: link it (link_source = 'rule'). Still several: never guess. Write a link_message approval for the advisor whose inbox received it, with one work.approval_link_options row per deal they are on (core.mandate_team); if they are on none, it goes to each deal's owner instead, so the dialog never shows a deal name to someone outside its team. The advisor picks one deal, several ("Both"), or "Not about a deal" (link_source = 'user'). It shows as overdue on Home after one working day.

  6. No match: no touchpoint; the message stays in the inbox only.

While a link_message approval is pending, the email has no touchpoint, so each candidate deal's Last contact waits for the choice; the decision writes one touchpoint per chosen deal (unique on email_message_id, mandate_id), and "Not about a deal" writes one with no mandate. A reply from someone in a tie pauses follow-ups on every candidate deal at once, before the choice, so no follow-up goes to a person who has already answered. Drafts written for one deal use only that deal's facts, never those of another deal the person is on. Meetings stay on one deal: Scribe asks for it when it writes the summary, and its picker lists only the deals the person recording is on.

Every claim has a source. Whatever the web shows, a value or an AI-written sentence, can open a source chip with the exact passage it came from, even if the website has since changed, because the page itself is a raw input kept forever.

ClaimPoints atRule the database enforces
A field's value from an outside source (Diffbot, PDL, Firecrawl, Google Places, Apollo, Scribe, Gmail)intake.field_sources.evidence_idRequired unless a person typed it or it came from Attio; a typed value points at the event naming who typed it
A proposed change, an approvalevidence_idRequired (approvals raised by a rule, such as a follow-up due, are exempt)
A comp or an unverified web multipleevidence_id: the dataset row or the saved pageRequired
A business blurb sentencecore.mandate_blurb_citationsAn approved blurb with no citation is refused at commit
A morning brief linework.daily_brief_item_citationsEvery line needs one
A Scribe decision, action item, claim or riskcomms.meeting_summary_item_citations (transcript lines)Every one needs one
Why a search result matchedintake.search_candidate_citationsWritten with the candidate
LinkedIn scans and signalsevidence_id on the kept enrichment tablesRequired

A citation is one audit.evidence row: the raw input, where in it the passage sits (a JSON path for an API response, a character range for a web page, a row for a spreadsheet, a page for a PDF, transcript segments for a meeting), the quote, the public URL and when it was captured. Evidence is append-only. The web reads one view, audit.v_evidence_card, through GET /api/v1/evidence/{id}.

Every live Attio attribute (read 10 Nov 2026) has exactly one home in Postgres, and a nightly drift check fails loudly when Attio gains a field we do not map.

Deal stages: two maps from the same Attio titles. Since 14 Nov, Deal_V2 holds 10 stages (Lead, Qualified, Engaged, Mandate signed, Preparation, Outreach, Non-binding offers, Due diligence, Closing, Closed) and a separate deal_status (Active, On hold, Passed, Lost).

  • A mandate keeps its stage through ref.attio_stage_map, which turns any title, old or new, into one of the 10 stages. Teaser Distributed, NDA Circulated, NDA Signed and CIM Distributed all become Outreach, because that detail now lives on each buyer. On Hold, Passed, Lost and Failed are statuses, not stages: the mandate keeps its last real stage from history (Lead if none) and takes that status. Closed is a stage whose status stays Active.

  • A legacy buyer–seller pair deal is not a mandate. It becomes a counterparty, and its old title sets the counterparty status instead (for example NDA Signed → Initial conversations with nda_signed_on set, LOI Received → LOI); that map waits for the counterparty statuses to be confirmed.

  • Read old titles from history. The 14 Nov switch collapses those titles into Outreach in Attio, so the backfill takes each deal's last title before 14 Nov from public.deal_stage_events, which kept the old values.

How sync stays exact

  • audit.attio_field_map holds one row per Attio attribute: object or list, slug, target table and column (or junction), and direction. The outbox writer and the webhook projector read it, so mapping lives in data, not scattered code.

  • ref.select_options and the dedicated ref tables carry attio_option_title for every Attio select option. A nightly job pulls Attio's attribute definitions and options, and alerts on any attribute or option missing from the map. The MCP read returns at most 20 options per attribute, so Richu loads full option lists through the Attio API, not the MCP.

  • Synced tables carry attio_record_id or attio_entry_id (unique), attio_synced_at and is_test. Postgres is the record: our change goes out through attio_outbox; an Attio-side edit to an owned field lands in intake as a proposal, never as a silent overwrite.

  • Money in Attio is USD, and so is every money column here: *_usd numeric(18,2). Comps and mandate financials are converted to USD when loaded; only offers also keep the LOI's own amount and currency.

Every index in the DDL serves either a foreign key or one of these screens; nothing is indexed "just in case". Targets are p95 under 50 ms at the seeded volume (50,000 organisations, 100,000 people, 300 mandates, 15,000 counterparties, 1 million events, 300,000 email messages).

The three hardest queries, written out so Richu can test their plans:

-- Outreach: my counterparties, latest touchpoint and follow-up state.
SELECT c.id, o.name, c.status_code, t.occurred_at AS last_touch, t.direction, s.next_follow_up_on
FROM core.counterparties c
JOIN core.organizations o ON o.id = c.organization_id
LEFT JOIN LATERAL (SELECT occurred_at, direction FROM comms.touchpoints
                   WHERE counterparty_id = c.id ORDER BY occurred_at DESC LIMIT 1) t ON true
LEFT JOIN outreach.v_counterparty_sequence s ON s.counterparty_id = c.id
WHERE c.owner_user_id = $1 AND c.removed_at IS NULL AND c.status_code <> 'passed';

-- Home: actionable threads, overdue when the last inbound is 24 h old with no later outbound.
SELECT th.id, th.subject, m.last_in, m.last_out,
       (m.last_in < now() - interval '24 hours' AND (m.last_out IS NULL OR m.last_out < m.last_in)) AS overdue
FROM comms.thread_triage tr
JOIN comms.email_threads th ON th.id = tr.thread_id
CROSS JOIN LATERAL (SELECT max(sent_at) FILTER (WHERE direction = 'inbound')  AS last_in,
                           max(sent_at) FILTER (WHERE direction = 'outbound') AS last_out
                    FROM comms.email_messages WHERE thread_id = th.id) m
WHERE tr.user_id = $1 AND tr.state = 'open' AND tr.is_actionable
ORDER BY m.last_in DESC;

-- Multiples: median and range from verified comps.
SELECT count(*) AS n,
       percentile_cont(0.5) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY ev_ebitda) AS median,
       min(ev_ebitda) AS low, max(ev_ebitda) AS high
FROM market.comps
WHERE is_verified AND removed_at IS NULL
  AND sector_code = $1 AND country_code = ANY($2) AND deal_on >= $3 AND ev_ebitda IS NOT NULL
  AND id <> ALL($4);                                  -- rows the advisor excluded

Operations

Volumes are small (tens of thousands of organisations, about a million events a year), so the work is in correctness and safe operation, not scale tricks.

Queues (PGMQ)

  • Installed by an Alembic revision from the pgmq install SQL into schema pgmq; no RDS extension needed. The SQL is the pgmq.sql bundled with pgmq-py 1.1.4 (PGMQ 1.13.0, which has the FIFO read functions). A SQL-only install cannot be upgraded in place, so a newer PGMQ is a new revision. Queues are created by the app's initialize(), never by hand.

  • Queues: import_jobs, attio_outbox, enrichment_jobs, outreach_followups, gmail_sync, calendar_sync, briefs, document_jobs, dataroom_events, nudges, plus one <name>_failed queue each.

  • Queue tables churn, so set autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor = 0.01 and autovacuum_vacuum_cost_delay = 0 on each queue table. Archived messages are purged after 30 days by a pg_cron job.

Connections

  • No RDS Proxy: workers long-poll PGMQ on held connections, and any later LISTEN/NOTIFY would break behind a transaction-mode proxy; two app instances do not need one.

  • Budget against max_connections = 200: API 2 instances × (pool 10 + overflow 5) = 30; workers 2 × 10 = 20; listeners 1 per queue per instance = 20; migrations and admin 10. Alarm at 70%.

  • Session settings per role: statement_timeout 15 s for the API role and 5 min for workers; idle_in_transaction_session_timeout 60 s; lock_timeout 5 s in migrations.

Size and retention

  • No partitioning at launch. audit.events and comms.email_messages get a BRIN index on their time column; revisit monthly range partitions at 50 million rows.

  • Kept for good: records, the event log, field-level changes, every raw input as received (webhooks, uploads, lead submissions, recordings), decisions, sends and approvals (DFSA record-keeping). Raw inputs are stored byte-for-byte in Postgres (up to 50 MB each) with their SHA-256, so one backup and one restore cover everything; at our volume that is a few GB a year.

  • Purged by pg_cron: PGMQ archives after 30, idempotency keys after 7, expired sessions daily. pg_cron also sends the scheduled messages to PGMQ (scheduled_jobs, briefs, nudges); each schedule is added in the revision of the phase that needs it.

  • Email bodies and transcripts are never stored in these tables: metadata and a 200-character snippet only, the body fetched on demand.

Backups and restore

  • RDS automated backups with point-in-time recovery, retention 35 days; a manual snapshot before every migration that rewrites a table.

  • A restore drill each month into a scratch instance, timed, with row counts checked (the PRD's Step 0 restore test).

Roles

RoleCanUsed by
wusool_ownerOwns every schema; DDLAlembic in the deploy workflow only
wusool_appSELECT, INSERT, UPDATE on all schemas, DELETE only on queue, session and staging tablesAPI and workers
wusool_readonlySELECT on core, market, audit viewsReporting, later the Wusool MCP

Passwords live in Secrets Manager and rotate; default privileges are set so new tables need no extra grants.

Monitoring

  • pg_stat_statements and Performance Insights on; auto_explain logs plans over 500 ms in dev.

  • Alarms: connections over 70%, any transaction over 5 minutes, a queue's oldest message older than its limit, failed-queue depth above 0, storage over 80%.

  • Before a phase goes live, Richu runs EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) for that phase's key queries on seeded, realistic volume and pastes the plans in the PR.

Migration from today's database

The new schemas are built beside today's public tables, filled by repeatable backfills, and the old tables retire only once nothing reads them, so every step can be rolled back.

  1. Snapshot. Manual RDS snapshots of dev and prod, named pre-engine-schema-<date>, kept 90 days. Check: a restore of the prod snapshot into a scratch instance passes row counts.

  2. Upgrade to Postgres 18. RDS blue/green on dev first, then prod in a quiet window (switchover takes under a minute). Confirm vector, pg_trgm, citext, pg_cron and pg_stat_statements versions on the green side (vector is dropped before the upgrade: the tables that used it are empty on prod), update engine_version in the Terraform postgres stack and the local docker-compose.yml image to a Postgres 18 build with pgvector. Check: ./checks.sh passes against 18.

  3. Create the schemas. Revisions 0001–0015 are additive; nothing in public changes. Check: Alembic upgrade and downgrade both run clean on a disposable Postgres 18.

  4. Backfill, report mode first. One idempotent script per area (organisations, people, roles, mandates, notes, meetings, interactions, activities), keyed on the Attio id so it can rerun. Each prints counts and every row it could not place (unknown select option, a duplicate email, a domain owned by two organisations, a deal whose stage has no mapping, a client, counterparty or search-list entry whose company has no buyer or seller role yet, which the script proposes creating) and writes nothing until Jules or Richu signs off the report. Text arrays split into junction rows through ref.attio_option_map; the comma-separated domains text splits into organization_domains. Before the first writing run, turn on the projector's writes to core (step 5), so no Attio change made during a long backfill is missed; both upsert on the Attio id, so their overlap is harmless. Report mode runs in the week of 1 Dec, and the writing run is on 15 Dec.

  5. Keep core current. The Attio webhook projector and the nightly resync write core alongside the old mirror. The app also writes core and the old table in one transaction through one helper in the crm module, keyed on the Attio id, for the shared entities only: organizations, people, buyer and seller roles, deals, notes, meetings and interactions. Until the buyer and seller writes move into crm, Slack and MCP writes reach core through the projector. A nightly reconcile compares counts and a field hash per record between Attio, the mirror and core, and alerts on any gap. Mail and calendar are already flowing: PR #396 fills public.interactions, interaction_participants and mailbox_sync_cursors through Google domain-wide delegation. The comms backfill copies those rows, after which the poll pass puts new items on gmail_sync and calendar_sync instead. Its 12-month purge stays off, because mail is kept until a retention period is decided.

  6. Switch readers. A feature's readers, the Engine pages first, move to core only after that feature is verified on dev with the dual write on; the rest move on 15 to 24 Dec. Existing modules (matching, discovery, enrichment, Scribe) move their reads to core one at a time, each behind its own PR with tests.

  7. Switch writers once, on 15 to 24 Dec. After the backfill is verified, core becomes the record, the dual-write helper is deleted and attio_outbox updates Attio. The old mirror stops receiving writes.

  8. Retire the mirror. After Attio retires (Q1), rename public mirror tables to legacy_*, wait 30 days, then drop them with a final snapshot.

Rollback: until step 7, pointing a feature's readers back at public restores today's behaviour at once, because the dual write keeps public current. After step 7, the outbox can be paused while Attio-first writes are switched back on for a day; the event log shows every change made in between.

Definition of done and open questions

A revision is done when every box below is ticked in its PR.

  • alembic upgrade head and alembic downgrade -1 both run clean on a disposable Postgres 18, and ./checks.sh schema passes.

  • Every foreign key has an explicit ON DELETE and an index; a CI query on pg_constraint finds none missing.

  • Every table with updated_at has the trigger; append-only tables have util.forbid_change().

  • Seeded at the target volume, the key queries for that phase show their planned index in EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS), pasted in the PR.

  • audit.attio_field_map covers every live attribute the revision touches, and the drift check is green.

  • Backfill report signed off; reconcile shows zero gaps for three nights in a row.

  • ORM models (SQLAlchemy 2, typed) and Pydantic schemas match the DDL; architecture tests pass.

  • GitBook's database page and CHANGELOG.md updated.

Open questions

  • Attio scorecard "Met" fields still point at the archived people and companies objects. Repoint them to person and organizations in Attio before phase 8?

  • Attio person emails are not unique. When the backfill finds two people with one email, do we merge them in Attio first, or keep both and flag them?

  • Attio person has two organisation links (company and organization). When they disagree, which wins?

  • deal.data_room_substatus has no options. Retire it in Attio?

  • organizations.client_type is comma-separated text. Turn it back into a multi-select in Attio so it can become a junction table?

  • The MCP returned 20 options at most per select. Richu pulls the full option lists from the Attio API for the seed; confirm he has an API key.

  • Which day does a scorecard week start on, Monday or Sunday?

  • Is Postgres 18 available on RDS in eu-central-1 for our instance class? If not, ship on 17 with gen_random_uuid() and switch the default to uuidv7() after the upgrade. Answered 16 Nov: yes. RDS offers 18.1 to 18.6, db.t4g.micro runs it, and dev and prod (16.13) can upgrade straight to 18.3, 18.4 or 18.6.

  • Individual buyers: Attio's buyer role list only holds organisations, so a person who buys in their own name has no buyer role. The spec lets a buy-side mandate name a person as client instead. Should individual buyers get a holding organisation in Attio instead, so the role-first rule has no exception?

  • Counterparty statuses: the seed uses the eight statuses the Engine's Deal view already shows (Not contacted, Contacted, Initial conversations, LOI, Due diligence, Bidding offer, Closed, Passed). Confirm with the Wusool team whether more are needed, for example NDA sent or NDA signed (today an NDA is only a date on the counterparty), and whether Bidding offer comes before or after LOI.

DDL

Postgres 18. Run in order; each block is one Alembic revision. Every table also gets created_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(), updated_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now() and the util.set_updated_at() trigger (left out below for readability), except append-only logs, which have no updated_at. The 8 tables whose indexes name created_at (import_batches, field_proposals, drafts, approvals, notification_actions, bottlenecks, skill_versions, record_changes) declare it themselves below, so it is not added twice.

0. Foundation (phase 0, by 20 Nov)

Schemas follow the backend modules, so a module owns its tables and the architecture tests can check imports against them.

SchemaHolds
refLookup tables: stages, statuses, sectors, geographies, FX rates
coreUsers, organisations, people, buyer and seller roles, mandates, counterparties
intakeImport staging, search runs, value provenance
marketComps and web comp results
commsConnections, email, calendar, touchpoints
outreachDrafts, recipients, approval batches. A separate usage schema holds every provider's spend and budgets
workApprovals, tasks, briefs, notifications, workstreams, bottlenecks
docsMaterials, documents, offers, skills
dataroomVantageKit links and activity
firmScorecards and partners
auditEvent log, Attio sync state, sessions, idempotency, rate limits. The analytics schema beside it holds precomputed summaries (section 8)
pgmqQueues (installed SQL)
-- rev 0001_foundation
CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS citext;
CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS pg_trgm;
-- vector is not installed: no new table uses it, and the legacy embedding tables, empty on prod (checked 16 Nov), are dropped first        
CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS pg_stat_statements;
CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS pg_cron;       -- maintenance jobs, and schedules that only call pgmq.send

CREATE SCHEMA ref; CREATE SCHEMA core; CREATE SCHEMA intake; CREATE SCHEMA market;
CREATE SCHEMA comms; CREATE SCHEMA outreach; CREATE SCHEMA work; CREATE SCHEMA docs;
CREATE SCHEMA dataroom; CREATE SCHEMA firm; CREATE SCHEMA audit; CREATE SCHEMA util;

-- Keeps updated_at honest on every UPDATE.
CREATE FUNCTION util.set_updated_at() RETURNS trigger LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$
BEGIN NEW.updated_at := now(); RETURN NEW; END $$;

-- Usage on each table with updated_at:
-- CREATE TRIGGER trg_<table>_updated_at BEFORE UPDATE ON <schema>.<table>
--   FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION util.set_updated_at();

-- Roles (passwords from Secrets Manager, set outside the migration).
-- Dev and prod already have wusool_app as the app's login role, so each role is created only if missing.
DO $$ BEGIN
  IF NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM pg_roles WHERE rolname = 'wusool_owner') THEN CREATE ROLE wusool_owner NOLOGIN; END IF;
  IF NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM pg_roles WHERE rolname = 'wusool_app') THEN CREATE ROLE wusool_app NOLOGIN; END IF;
  IF NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM pg_roles WHERE rolname = 'wusool_readonly') THEN CREATE ROLE wusool_readonly NOLOGIN; END IF;
END $$;
GRANT wusool_owner TO CURRENT_USER;   -- the migration user can then SET ROLE wusool_owner, so it owns every object
GRANT USAGE ON SCHEMA ref, core, intake, market, comms, outreach, work, docs, dataroom, firm, audit, util TO wusool_app;
-- Default privileges only apply to tables created by the named owner, so name it.
ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES FOR ROLE wusool_owner IN SCHEMA ref, core, intake, market, comms, outreach, work, docs, dataroom, firm, audit
  GRANT SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE ON TABLES TO wusool_app;
ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES FOR ROLE wusool_owner IN SCHEMA util GRANT EXECUTE ON FUNCTIONS TO wusool_app;
GRANT USAGE ON SCHEMA ref, core, market, audit TO wusool_readonly;
ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES FOR ROLE wusool_owner IN SCHEMA ref, core, market, audit GRANT SELECT ON TABLES TO wusool_readonly;
-- DELETE only where rows are meant to go: staging, sessions, idempotency, rate limits
-- (granted per table in the revision that creates it). The three pgmq grants below
-- belong at the end of rev 0002, once the pgmq schema exists.
GRANT USAGE ON SCHEMA pgmq TO wusool_app;
GRANT SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE ON ALL TABLES IN SCHEMA pgmq TO wusool_app;
GRANT EXECUTE ON ALL FUNCTIONS IN SCHEMA pgmq TO wusool_app;
-- Timeouts belong on the LOGIN roles (group-role settings are not inherited):
DO $$ BEGIN IF NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM pg_roles WHERE rolname = 'wusool_api') THEN CREATE ROLE wusool_api LOGIN IN ROLE wusool_app; END IF; END $$;     DO $$ BEGIN IF NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM pg_roles WHERE rolname = 'wusool_worker') THEN CREATE ROLE wusool_worker LOGIN IN ROLE wusool_app; END IF; END $$;
ALTER ROLE wusool_api SET statement_timeout = '15s';
ALTER ROLE wusool_worker SET statement_timeout = '5min';
ALTER ROLE wusool_api SET idle_in_transaction_session_timeout = '60s';
ALTER ROLE wusool_worker SET idle_in_transaction_session_timeout = '60s';
-- Every instant is stored and read in UTC; Dubai time is applied on display only.
ALTER ROLE wusool_api SET timezone = 'UTC';
ALTER ROLE wusool_worker SET timezone = 'UTC';
-- rev 0002_pgmq: apply the pgmq install SQL bundled with pgmq-py 1.1.4 (PGMQ 1.13.0,
-- has read_grouped) into schema pgmq.
-- Downgrade drops nothing: queues hold live work. SQL-only installs cannot upgrade in
-- place, so a newer PGMQ is a new revision.
-- pg_cron schedules are added in each phase's revision, for example
-- SELECT cron.schedule_in_database('brief-0730-dubai', '30 3 * * *',
--   $$SELECT pgmq.send('briefs', '{"job":"daily_brief"}')$$, '<app database>');

1. ref: lookups (phase 0, by 20 Nov)

Dedicated tables for values the Engine reasons about (stages, statuses, sectors, countries). Display-only Attio selects share ref.select_options, enforced with a composite foreign key so each column only accepts its own set.

-- rev 0003_ref
-- Money is stored in USD (*_usd numeric(18,2)); offers alone also keep the LOI's own currency.
-- These rates are used only when a non-USD figure is entered, never in views.
CREATE TABLE ref.fx_rates (
  currency char(3) NOT NULL CHECK (currency ~ '^[A-Z]{3}$'),
  valid_from date NOT NULL,
  usd_per_unit numeric(18,8) NOT NULL CHECK (usd_per_unit > 0),
  PRIMARY KEY (currency, valid_from));          -- AED = 1/3.6725

CREATE TABLE ref.regions (code text PRIMARY KEY, label text NOT NULL, attio_option_title text UNIQUE);
CREATE TABLE ref.countries (
  code char(2) PRIMARY KEY CHECK (code ~ '^[A-Z]{2}$'),     -- ISO 3166-1
  name text NOT NULL,
  region_code text NOT NULL REFERENCES ref.regions ON DELETE RESTRICT,
  risk_adjustment_pct numeric(5,2) NOT NULL DEFAULT 0 CHECK (risk_adjustment_pct BETWEEN -100 AND 100),
  attio_option_title text UNIQUE);
CREATE INDEX ix_countries_region ON ref.countries (region_code);

CREATE TABLE ref.sectors (
  code text PRIMARY KEY, label text NOT NULL UNIQUE,

CREATE INDEX ix_sectors_parent ON ref.sectors (parent_code);

-- Each Attio select maps option titles onto our codes; one row per attribute + option.
CREATE TABLE ref.attio_option_map (
  attio_parent text NOT NULL,            -- object or list slug
  attio_attribute text NOT NULL,         -- e.g. sector_focus, target_vertical, sector
  attio_option_title text NOT NULL,
  ref_table text NOT NULL,               -- e.g. ref.sectors
  ref_code text NOT NULL,
  PRIMARY KEY (attio_parent, attio_attribute, attio_option_title));

CREATE TABLE ref.organization_types (code text PRIMARY KEY, label text NOT NULL UNIQUE, is_active boolean NOT NULL DEFAULT true);
CREATE TABLE ref.investment_stages  (code text PRIMARY KEY, label text NOT NULL UNIQUE, is_active boolean NOT NULL DEFAULT true);
CREATE TABLE ref.categories         (code text PRIMARY KEY, label text NOT NULL UNIQUE, is_active boolean NOT NULL DEFAULT true);
CREATE TABLE ref.person_roles       (code text PRIMARY KEY, label text NOT NULL UNIQUE, is_active boolean NOT NULL DEFAULT true);
-- Access control: roles grant permissions; users hold roles (core.user_roles);
-- deal-level access comes from core.mandate_team.
CREATE TABLE ref.roles (code text PRIMARY KEY, label text NOT NULL, description text NOT NULL);
  -- seed: admin, advisor, analyst, ops
CREATE TABLE ref.permissions (
  code text PRIMARY KEY CHECK (code ~ '^[a-z_]+\.[a-z_]+$'), description text NOT NULL);
  -- seed: deals.view_all, deals.view_staffed, deals.edit, outreach.send, approvals.decide,
  -- providers.spend, fees.view, skills.edit, partners.publish, users.manage, imports.approve
CREATE TABLE ref.role_permissions (
  role_code text REFERENCES ref.roles ON DELETE CASCADE,
  permission_code text REFERENCES ref.permissions ON DELETE CASCADE,
  PRIMARY KEY (role_code, permission_code));
CREATE INDEX ix_role_permissions_permission ON ref.role_permissions (permission_code);

-- Engine pipeline: 10 stages in order, 4 statuses (PRD stage migration).
CREATE TABLE ref.mandate_stages (
  code text PRIMARY KEY, label text NOT NULL UNIQUE,
  position smallint NOT NULL UNIQUE CHECK (position BETWEEN 1 AND 10),
  phase text NOT NULL CHECK (phase IN ('opportunity','mandate')));
CREATE TABLE ref.mandate_statuses (code text PRIMARY KEY CHECK (code IN ('active','on_hold','passed','lost')), label text NOT NULL);
CREATE TABLE ref.attio_stage_map (
  attio_stage_title text PRIMARY KEY,
  stage_code text REFERENCES ref.mandate_stages ON DELETE RESTRICT,     -- NULL: last real stage from history (Lead if none)
  status_code text REFERENCES ref.mandate_statuses ON DELETE RESTRICT,  -- NULL: read Attio's deal_status (Active when absent)
  CHECK ((stage_code IS NULL) <> (status_code IS NULL)),
  is_canonical boolean NOT NULL DEFAULT false);   -- the one title we write back per stage
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX uq_attio_stage_map_canonical ON ref.attio_stage_map (stage_code) WHERE is_canonical;
